arXiv 2604.17335 · IEEE RA-L 2026

Learning Whole-Body Humanoid Locomotion via Motion Generation and Motion Tracking

Zewei Zhang, Kehan Wen, Michael Xu, Junzhe He, Chenhao Li, Takahiro Miki, Clemens Schwarke, Chong Zhang, Xue Bin Peng, Marco Hutter · ETH Zurich RSL, SFU, EPFL, NVIDIA

A diffusion model sketches the next 0.5 s of human-style motion from the terrain ahead. An RL tracker turns that sketch into joint commands. What makes it work on a real Unitree G1: fine-tune the tracker while it follows the generator's own imperfect output.

Two ways to train a humanoid, each missing half

ApproachWhole-body, human-like motionAdapts to terrain online
RL with hand-made rewardsNo: legs do everything, arms idleYes

Overview

Three stages

Stage a · Data

From 5 minutes of human clips to 1 hour of robot motion

One clip per skill to start: climb a 50 cm box, vault a 35 cm hurdle, jump down 50 cm, stairs at ≈20 cm, plus walking and turning.

  1. CaptureOwn videos → 3D human motion with GVHMR; plus AMASS and OmniRetarget clips.
  2. RetargetMap to the G1 with contact-constrained inverse kinematics (IK: solve joint angles that put hands and feet where the human's were).
  3. Place terrainPut boxes and hurdles by hand where the human touched them.
  4. CleanTrain a DeepMimic-style tracker on the clips and keep what the simulated robot actually did. This drops physically impossible frames.
  5. AugmentScale obstacle heights, drop small boxes on the path, re-optimize motion with penetration and smoothness losses.
  6. Clean againTrack the augmented clips in sim, record the result. ≈1 h of data.
Stage b · Motion generator

A diffusion model that sketches the next half second

What it computes \[ \hat{\mathbf X}_{t+1:t+25} = G_\theta\big(\mathbf d,\ \mathbf h_t,\ \mathbf s_{t-1},\ \mathbf s_t\big) \] \[ 99 = \underbrace{3}_{\text{root pos}} + \underbrace{4}_{\text{quat}} + \underbrace{23}_{\text{joints}} + \underbrace{23{\times}3}_{\text{link pos}} \] Notation is mine; the paper describes this in words.
Training loss (standard MDM form) \[ \mathbf X^{(k)} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}\,\mathbf X^{(0)} + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\,\boldsymbol\epsilon \] \[ \mathcal L = \big\lVert G_\theta(\mathbf X^{(k)}, k, \mathbf c) - \mathbf X^{(0)} \big\rVert^2 + \mathcal L_{\text{vel}} + \mathcal L_{\text{joint}} + \mathcal L_{\text{pen}} \] MDM predicts the clean motion \(\mathbf X^{(0)}\) directly. The paper names the extra losses (velocity, joint consistency, terrain penetration, as in PARC) but not their formulas or weights.

Robustness trick: during training the height scan and the 2 past frames are perturbed with noise, so the generator copes with a noisy real robot state.

Stage b · Motion tracker

An RL policy that follows the sketch

Pre-training reward · paper Eq. 1 \[ R_{\text{pre}} = r_{\text{mimic}} + r_{\text{reg}} \tag{1} \]
GroupTermEquation (\(^*\) = reference)
r_mimicBase pose\(3\exp\!\big(-4\lVert \mathbf p_b^w-\mathbf p_b^{w*}\rVert^2 - \lVert \mathbf q_b \otimes {\mathbf q_b^{*}}^{-1}\rVert^2\big)\)
Base velocity\(\exp\!\big(-\lVert \mathbf v_b^b-\mathbf v_b^{b*}\rVert^2 - 0.1\lVert \boldsymbol\omega_b^b-\boldsymbol\omega_b^{b*}\rVert^2\big)\)
Joint position\(2.5\exp\!\big(-2\sum_{i=1}^{23}0.25\,(q_i-q_i^*)^2\big)\)
Joint velocity\(0.5\exp\!\big(-2\sum_{i=1}^{23}0.01\,(\dot q_i-\dot q_i^*)^2\big)\)
Key bodies (base frame)\(2\exp\!\big(-\sum_{i=1}^{9}\lVert \mathbf p_{l,i}^b-\mathbf p_{l,i}^{b*}\rVert^2\big)\)
Key bodies (world)\(\exp\!\big(-\sum_{i=1}^{9}\lVert \mathbf p_{l,i}^w-\mathbf p_{l,i}^{w*}\rVert^2\big)\)
r_regAction rate (1st order)\(-0.1\sum_i (a_{t,i}-a_{t-1,i})^2\)
Action rate (2nd order)\(-0.05\sum_i (a_{t,i}-2a_{t-1,i}+a_{t-2,i})^2\)
Joint position limits\(-10\sum_i \max(q_i-q_{\text{lim},i},\,0)\)
Joint velocity limits\(-\sum_i \max(\dot q_i-\dot q_{\text{lim},i},\,0)\)
Torque limits\(-0.001\sum_i \max(\tau_i-\tau_{\text{lim},i},\,0)\)
Joint torques\(-10^{-5}\sum_i \tau_i^2\)
Body acceleration\(-0.01\sum_{i=1}^{9}\lVert \ddot{\mathbf p}_{l,i}^{w}\rVert^2\)
r_taskHeading (fine-tuning only)\(1.5\,\langle \mathbf v_b^b, \mathbf d_b\rangle / \lVert \mathbf v_b^b\rVert\)

Superscripts: \(w\) world frame, \(b\) base frame. \(\mathbf p_{l,i}\) are 9 key bodies (hands, feet, etc.). On the quaternion term: taken literally the norm of a unit quaternion is always 1, so read it as the size of the orientation error.

Stage c · Closed-loop fine-tuning

Freeze the generator, train the tracker on its output

Fine-tuning reward · paper Eq. 2 \[ R_{\text{post}} = r_{\text{mimic}} + r_{\text{reg}} + r_{\text{task}} \tag{2} \] \[ r_{\text{task}} = 1.5\,\frac{\langle \mathbf v_b^b,\ \mathbf d_b\rangle}{\lVert \mathbf v_b^b\rVert} = 1.5\cos\theta \] \(\theta\) is the angle between where the base moves and where it should go. Example: 30° off gives \(1.5\cos 30^\circ = 1.30\); walking backward gives −1.5. Speed does not matter, only direction.
Harder terrain than the data
  • Stairs, 15–25 cm steps
  • Several hurdles in a row, 25–55 cm
  • Boxes and pyramid steps, 30–85 cm, random width, yaw and pitch
  • Random goal direction; noise on generator inputs and tracker observations
New behaviors not in the clips: climbing a box at its corner, turning on top before jumping down, vaulting hurdles back to back.

What the tracker saw in pre-training

Smooth, physics-cleaned clips from the dataset.

What it sees with the generator

References built from a noisy robot state with only 2 denoising steps. They can jump between frames or slide the feet.

Fine-tuning closes that gap. The tracker learns to follow the gist of the reference and ignore the unsafe parts, so it acts as a motion filter on the generator's output.

Deployment

Everything runs on the robot

Results

Both parts are needed

Takeaways

What to remember

  • Split planning from control. The generator decides what whole-body motion fits the terrain; the tracker decides how to do it with real physics.
  • Train the tracker on the generator's real output. A tracker trained only on clean clips breaks on generated references (Fig. 4). Closed-loop fine-tuning fixes this.
  • Small data goes far. 5 min of human clips, augmented to 1 h, plus random terrain in RL, covers boxes up to 85 cm and new terrain combinations.
  • Limit: it depends on a good LiDAR height map. When the map is noisy, performance drops a lot. The authors suggest neural mapping or a belief encoder (an estimator that falls back on body sensing when vision fails), and loco-manipulation next.
